newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria cabinet endorses ban on religious party base.
newsitem.headline: Algeria cabinet endorses ban on religious party base.

text.p: The Algerian cabinet, in a swift follow-up to constitutional change, on Wednesday approved a draft law banning political parties based on religion, language or regions.
The official Algerian news agency APS, in a statement on the cabinet meeting, said the new law also laid the basis for proportional representation for a general election promised for early next year.
The draft law follows a November referendum to change the constitution. It was approved by 84.6 percent of voters and signed into law by President Liamine Zeroual this month.

Algeria has been engaged in a five-year-old conflict with Moslem fundamentalists since shortly after the authorities in January 1992 cancelled a general election in which the Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) had taken a huge lead.
The FIS was later banned. About 60,000 people have been killed in the conflict, with 20 bus passengers being murdered on Wednesday in the latest attack blamed on Moslem guerrillas.
Existing legal parties, such as Hamas and Nahda whose fundamental principles are religious, have a year from the date the law is promulgated to change their base.
The statement did not indicate whether these parties would be able to participate in the ballot which President Liamine Zeroual has said would be held in the first-half of 1997.
"The prohibited bases and objectives for the creation and action of all political parties...are as follows:
-- practices contrary to the values of Islamic moral, of national identity and the values of the November 1, 1954 Revolution and which affect the symbols of the republic.
"In this framework, a political party may not, moreover, found its creation or its action on a religious, linguistic, racial, sexist, corporatist or regionalist base," the draft said.
The draft stipulates that parties must respect "alternance of power by way of the free choice" of Algeria's 29 million people.
Deputy FIS leader Ali Belhadj, now serving a 12-year jail term, had vowed in the run-up to the later-scrapped election that if the FIS won power it would hold onto it.

Under the new law, any party wanting registration must hold a constituent congress of 400 to 500 people elected by 2,500 supporters from at least 25 of the North African country's 48 "wilayas" or provinces.

Two of the main secular opposition parties, the Socialist Forces Front (FFS) and the Rally for Culture and Democracy (RCD), whose stronghold is in the Berber Kabylie region in northeast Algeria, see the changes as a threat to their existence.

FFS leader, independence war veteran Hocine Ait Ahmed said last month: "The new constitution provides weapons to the president to control, manipulate and dissolve the political parties. The authorities can obviously find any pretext to ban our party."
The FFS came a distant second to the FIS in the December 1991 first round general election, scrapped one month later.
Algeria has had no elected parliament since 1992 and draft laws approved by cabinet are submitted to the government- appointed National Transitional Council for debate.
